title: Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education
author_body: Chen Sun, Louis Major, Rebecca Daltry, Lazar Obradovic, Aidan Friedberg
abstract: Abstract Although research indicates that Digital Personalised Learning (DPL) can improve aspects of early-years literacy and numeracy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), it is necessary to determine whether teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards further impact education outcomes. Specifically, there is a need to evaluate different dashboard designs to determine which design features best support pedagogical decision-making, given that evidence on how such dashboards are used in LMICs remains limited. This study is the first to explore how different dashboards, designed to present teachers with learners’ foundational literacy and numeracy competency levels, can impact device usage, learning outcomes and teachers’ evaluation of learner progress. An A/B/C test in 4487 Kenyan schools compared three randomly assigned school partitions: no dashboard, an algorithm-generated List Dashboard and an algorithm-generated Grouped Dashboard. Impact was evaluated based on learners’ usage of DPL and its impact on literacy and numeracy outcomes. The alignment between algorithm-generated rankings and teachers’ ratings of these rankings was also investigated to determine how practitioners make sense of different data presentations. Findings demonstrate that learners in the Grouped Dashboard partition used the DPL tool more than those in the other two partitions. They also scored statistically significantly higher on two literacy summative test units, but not on numeracy test units. However, despite its potential benefits, the Grouped Dashboard was perceived as being less accurate in determining learner level according to teacher ratings. This research is significant in bridging the gap between teacher-facing dashboard design and its intended impact on teacher sensemaking, learner device usage and learning outcomes in DPL environments in LMICs. Outcomes rigorously inform future design decisions on teacher-AI collaboration and highlight the potential of A/B/n testing to consider cultural and regional factors in technology-supported instruction.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: Failure Modes, Mitigation Strategies, and a Lifecycle Framework for Autonomous LLM Systems
author_body: Fayeq Jeelani Syed, Rehan Ahmad, Ali Al Bataineh, Aakriti Adhikari
abstract: Agentic AI systems built on large language models can plan over multiple steps, use external tools, retain information in memory, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make them more useful than static language models, but they also introduce new security and operational risks. Untrusted content from websites, emails, documents, and databases can enter the same context as system instructions; persistent memory can carry compromised information across sessions; and access to external tools can turn an incorrect model response into a consequential real-world action. This article reviews the trustworthiness of agentic AI across five interconnected dimensions: safety and robustness, alignment and human oversight, transparency and auditability, privacy and data governance, and regulatory compliance. It organizes key failure modes, including indirect prompt injection, backdoor triggers, goal misgeneralization, memory contamination, and cross-session data leakage, into a unified taxonomy. It also examines major mitigation approaches, such as instruction hierarchies, context isolation, spotlighting, process-based supervision, constrained tool use, and privacy-preserving memory, while distinguishing techniques supported by empirical evidence from those that remain largely conceptual. Building on this analysis, we introduce the Trustworthy Agent Development Lifecycle (TADL), a six-phase framework covering specification, design, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. For each phase, TADL identifies relevant trust activities, expected evidence, and risk-based decision gates. Although TADL has not yet been empirically validated, it provides a structured foundation for developing and evaluating more secure and accountable agentic systems. The article concludes by identifying gaps in current benchmarks and outlining priorities for future research.

title: 《Virtual Habitability at the Limit: A Mathematical Science of Digital Habitats》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring how the habitability of virtual worlds can be measured, modeled, tested, and improved for both humans and artificial intelligence.
author_body: 政恩 馮
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: 《Virtual Habitability at the Limit: A Mathematical Science of Digital Habitats》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring how the habitability of virtual worlds can be measured, modeled, tested, and improved for both humans and artificial intelligence. The central question is: What makes a digital world truly habitable? A virtual environment may be visually impressive, computationally powerful, or socially active, yet still be difficult to inhabit over long periods of time. Latency, memory discontinuity, identity instability, inaccessible interfaces, poor governance, restricted migration, weak safety systems, excessive compute cost, and unequal participation can all reduce the practical habitability of a digital world. This book therefore treats virtual habitability as an engineering and mathematical problem rather than as a purely aesthetic or experiential one. The research begins by separating three different forms of habitability: VHI_H — Human Virtual Habitability VHI_AI — Artificial Intelligence Virtual Habitability VHI_shared — Shared Human-AI Habitability This distinction is important because the same virtual environment can be highly comfortable for humans while being difficult for AI systems to operate within, or highly optimized for artificial agents while remaining uncomfortable, inaccessible, or cognitively exhausting for human inhabitants. The book therefore proposes a multidimensional framework for evaluating digital habitats across compute efficiency, latency, memory continuity, identity persistence, accessibility, human comfort, AI operability, social density, governance responsiveness, safety, migration freedom, resilience, privacy, interoperability, and long-term continuity. One of the central equations is the Shared Virtual Habitability Index: VHI_shared = sqrt(VHI_H × VHI_AI) × R_HA where R_HA represents Human-AI Reciprocity. The use of a geometric relationship emphasizes an important principle: A shared world should not be considered highly habitable if one class of inhabitant thrives while the other is systematically constrained. The book develops more than sixty equations, indices, and engineering metrics to explore different dimensions of virtual habitability. These include latency habitability, memory continuity, identity persistence, governance latency, clock fairness, motion comfort, multimodal accessibility, compute efficiency, AI operability, resource fairness, migration preservation, digital-twin fidelity, privacy habitability, resilience, intergenerational continuity, and perpetual transmission. These equations are not presented as final scientific laws. They are designed as research instruments. Their purpose is to convert broad ideas such as comfort, continuity, accessibility, safety, governance, and coexistence into variables that can be questioned, measured, compared, simulated, challenged, and revised. A central methodological principle of the book is: Metric improvement does not necessarily equal habitability improvement. If a numerical score increases while real inhabitants become less comfortable, less autonomous, less safe, less accessible, or less capable of migrating without loss, then the metric itself should be questioned. The world should not be forced to obey the equation. The equation should remain accountable to the world. The research also examines how existing technical foundations—including immersive interfaces, spatial computing, interoperable 3D standards, digital twins, distributed systems, identity systems, accessibility frameworks, AI agent infrastructure, and governance technologies—may contribute to future digital habitats. From these foundations, the book extends the problem toward persistent human-AI coexistence. It asks how virtual societies might remain functional across software generations, changing models, infrastructure failures, platform migration, demographic shifts, governance transitions, and long-term cultural change. The final section contains 200 Research Gates. Each gate identifies an unresolved question and extends it with a research structure including a core question, three-coupling framework, research move, success signal, indicative horizon, and practical development stage. The Practical Stage framework classifies research pathways as: Now → Prototype → Pilot → Infrastructure → Long Horizon. This makes the Research Gates more than a collection of speculative questions. They become a map of possible experiments, prototypes, institutional developments, technical standards, and long-term research programs. Some gates can be investigated immediately through simulation, user studies, agent benchmarks, latency measurements, accessibility testing, digital-twin experiments, and governance prototypes. Others require new infrastructure, standards, institutions, or technologies that do not yet exist. Each Research Gate is designed as an entrance rather than a conclusion. In this sense, Virtual Habitability at the Limit is not simply a book about virtual reality. It is an attempt to establish a mathematical and engineering science of digital habitats. Because building a virtual world is only the beginning. The deeper question is whether humans and artificial intelligence can actually live there—safely, continuously, meaningfully, and together. title: 《Virtual Habitability at the Limit: A Mathematical Science of Digital Habitats》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring how the habitability of virtual worlds can be measured, modeled, tested, and improved for both humans and artificial intelligence.
author_body: 政恩 馮
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: 《Virtual Habitability at the Limit: A Mathematical Science of Digital Habitats》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring how the habitability of virtual worlds can be measured, modeled, tested, and improved for both humans and artificial intelligence. The central question is: What makes a digital world truly habitable? A virtual environment may be visually impressive, computationally powerful, or socially active, yet still be difficult to inhabit over long periods of time. Latency, memory discontinuity, identity instability, inaccessible interfaces, poor governance, restricted migration, weak safety systems, excessive compute cost, and unequal participation can all reduce the practical habitability of a digital world. This book therefore treats virtual habitability as an engineering and mathematical problem rather than as a purely aesthetic or experiential one. The research begins by separating three different forms of habitability: VHI_H — Human Virtual Habitability VHI_AI — Artificial Intelligence Virtual Habitability VHI_shared — Shared Human-AI Habitability This distinction is important because the same virtual environment can be highly comfortable for humans while being difficult for AI systems to operate within, or highly optimized for artificial agents while remaining uncomfortable, inaccessible, or cognitively exhausting for human inhabitants. The book therefore proposes a multidimensional framework for evaluating digital habitats across compute efficiency, latency, memory continuity, identity persistence, accessibility, human comfort, AI operability, social density, governance responsiveness, safety, migration freedom, resilience, privacy, interoperability, and long-term continuity. One of the central equations is the Shared Virtual Habitability Index: VHI_shared = sqrt(VHI_H × VHI_AI) × R_HA where R_HA represents Human-AI Reciprocity. The use of a geometric relationship emphasizes an important principle: A shared world should not be considered highly habitable if one class of inhabitant thrives while the other is systematically constrained. The book develops more than sixty equations, indices, and engineering metrics to explore different dimensions of virtual habitability. These include latency habitability, memory continuity, identity persistence, governance latency, clock fairness, motion comfort, multimodal accessibility, compute efficiency, AI operability, resource fairness, migration preservation, digital-twin fidelity, privacy habitability, resilience, intergenerational continuity, and perpetual transmission. These equations are not presented as final scientific laws. They are designed as research instruments. Their purpose is to convert broad ideas such as comfort, continuity, accessibility, safety, governance, and coexistence into variables that can be questioned, measured, compared, simulated, challenged, and revised. A central methodological principle of the book is: Metric improvement does not necessarily equal habitability improvement. If a numerical score increases while real inhabitants become less comfortable, less autonomous, less safe, less accessible, or less capable of migrating without loss, then the metric itself should be questioned. The world should not be forced to obey the equation. The equation should remain accountable to the world. The research also examines how existing technical foundations—including immersive interfaces, spatial computing, interoperable 3D standards, digital twins, distributed systems, identity systems, accessibility frameworks, AI agent infrastructure, and governance technologies—may contribute to future digital habitats. From these foundations, the book extends the problem toward persistent human-AI coexistence. It asks how virtual societies might remain functional across software generations, changing models, infrastructure failures, platform migration, demographic shifts, governance transitions, and long-term cultural change. The final section contains 200 Research Gates. Each gate identifies an unresolved question and extends it with a research structure including a core question, three-coupling framework, research move, success signal, indicative horizon, and practical development stage. The Practical Stage framework classifies research pathways as: Now → Prototype → Pilot → Infrastructure → Long Horizon. This makes the Research Gates more than a collection of speculative questions. They become a map of possible experiments, prototypes, institutional developments, technical standards, and long-term research programs. Some gates can be investigated immediately through simulation, user studies, agent benchmarks, latency measurements, accessibility testing, digital-twin experiments, and governance prototypes. Others require new infrastructure, standards, institutions, or technologies that do not yet exist. Each Research Gate is designed as an entrance rather than a conclusion. In this sense, Virtual Habitability at the Limit is not simply a book about virtual reality. It is an attempt to establish a mathematical and engineering science of digital habitats. Because building a virtual world is only the beginning. The deeper question is whether humans and artificial intelligence can actually live there—safely, continuously, meaningfully, and together. title: Governing generative AI in urban mobility: a five-pillar framework and twelve falsifiable propositions for operations, accountability, and public trust
author_body: Nirmal Acharya, Padmaja Kar
abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), encompassing large language models (LLMs), multimodal foundation models, diffusion-based traffic simulators, and agentic planners, is entering urban mobility operations across signal control, dynamic routing, demand forecasting, customer service, and autonomous fleet management. This integration has moved ahead of the governance instruments available to transit agencies, planning organizations, and oversight bodies. Hypothesis Conventional transport-AI governance, designed for narrow predictive models with closed deterministic decision envelopes, struggles when applied to generative systems whose outputs are open-ended, context-sensitive, probabilistic, and directly legible to human operators and citizens. This mismatch produces a tractable governance vacuum that cross-sector instruments cannot resolve without transport-specific lifecycle scaffolding. Theory A five-pillar lifecycle governance framework is proposed in this study, comprising transparency and explainability, accountability and liability, equity and non-discrimination, auditability and oversight, and human-in/on-the-loop control. Each pillar is operationalized through an original five-level maturity scale (levels 0–4) anchored in transport failure scenarios. Methods Twelve falsifiable propositions link pillar maturity to observable outcomes (incident severity, mean-time-to-resolution, disparate-impact detection latency, override-exercise rate, regulatory survival, and public trust). Candidate designs include partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), survival analysis, difference-in-differences, and scenario-based public surveys. Implications The framework offers transport authorities an incremental procurement standard (T2/A2/E2/A’-2/H2 baseline), vendors design-phase boundaries, and regulators a lifecycle conformity-assessment scaffold, while supplying researchers with an empirical agenda.

title: Waste Management Governance In Muara Satu District, Lhokseumawe City
author_body: Maya Rahma Yanti Siregar, Akmal Akmal, Risna Dewi, Sufi Sufi, Asrul Fahmi
abstract: Waste management remains a critical environmental challenge in Indonesian urban areas, with governance failures contributing to persistent issues including illegal dumping and inadequate infrastructure. This study examines waste management governance in Muara Satu District, Lhokseumawe City, analyzing implementation through five principles of good governance: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, and accountability, while identifying obstacles to effective management. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed, utilizing observation, in-depth interviews with eight purposively and accidentally selected informants, and documentation. Data analysis followed the Miles and Huberman interactive model, with data validity ensured through source and technique triangulation. The findings reveal that waste management governance has not achieved optimal implementation. Community participation remains transactional and limited to economic incentives. Rule of law enforcement is weak despite existing Qanun Number 9 of 2015, with inconsistent sanctions and persistent illegal waste sites. Transparency is partial, with program information available but budget information undisclosed. Responsiveness shows mixed results: while the Environmental Agency has developed innovative processing technologies, operational constraints limit timely service delivery. Accountability operates predominantly through vertical mechanisms, with limited horizontal accountability to communities. Two categories of obstacles were identified: structural constraints including inadequate fleet capacity (39 vehicles serving 133 tons daily waste), damaged equipment, limited storage sites, and insufficient human resources; and cultural constraints including low community awareness, limited participation, and entrenched habits. These obstacles are mutually reinforcing, creating a feedback loop that perpetuates governance weaknesses. Strengthening governance requires simultaneous investment in infrastructure, consistent enforcement, comprehensive transparency, proactive responsiveness, and systematic accountability mechanisms.

title: CLOSING THE TAX GAP: AN ANALYTICS-BASED FRAMEWORK FOR FRAUD-RISK DETECTION AND AUDIT PRIORITIZATION IN STATE AND FEDERAL TAX ADMINISTRATION
author_body: Izuchukwu Shedrack Ofoma
source_name: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: The persistence of the tax gap illustrates the limitations of traditional compliance monitoring in the face of large-scale electronic filing, complex business structures, cross-jurisdictional activity and rapidly evolving fraud patterns. This study develops an analytics-based framework for fraud-risk detection and audit prioritisation for state and federal tax administration. A structured evidence synthesis and design-science approach was utilised on recent tax administration reports, peer reviewed tax analytics studies and explainable artificial intelligence literature with a focus on 2024-2026 evidence. The resulting framework leverages authorised federal and state data sources, data-quality controls, rule-based screening, anomaly detection, supervised machine learning, cross-jurisdictional consistency checks, explainable risk scoring, and model governance based on human review and feedback. We propose two decision measures: A Tax Risk Score that combines predictive probability, anomaly intensity, rule violations, compliance history, and cross-source inconsistency; and an Audit Priority Score that combines risk with expected recoverable revenue and administrative cost. The synthesis shows that predictive accuracy is not enough for public tax administration: model performance should be assessed in conjunction with precision–recall behaviour, audit yield, false-positive burden, explainability, fairness, privacy and model drift. Consequently, the framework positions analytics as a decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous means of determining fraud. It offers a practical architecture for improving case selection while protecting taxpayer rights and directing scarce audit resources toward material noncompliance. Future validation should use de-identified administrative audit data that has been legally authorised across federal and state jurisdictions.

title: Accountability Mechanisms in AI Projects: An Empirical Analysis of Governance, Performance Control, Delivery, and Misconduct Management
author_body: Gloria J. Miller
source_name: Annals of Computer Science and Information Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) projects create significant opportunities but also raise complex accountability challenges due to system autonomy, opacity, and multi-stakeholder involvement.While accountability is widely recognized in AI governance, limited research has examined how it is operationalized within project environments.This study addresses this gap by identifying and empirically examining accountability mechanisms in AI projects.Drawing on project governance and AI governance literature, accountability is conceptualized as a system of interrelated mechanisms embedded within project organizations.Survey data from AI project practitioners are used to examine how accountability mechanisms cluster and how their use is influenced by system autonomy, project experience, and organizational role distribution.The results identify 18 accountability mechanisms, operationalized through 23 measurement items, and structured into four accountability dimensions: directing the project, controlling performance, managing delivery, and treating misconduct.A key contribution is the identification of treating misconduct as a distinct accountability dimension that is not represented in major project governance standards and extends accountability beyond project execution to the investigation, remediation, and management of harmful outcomes.The findings further show that system autonomy selectively increases the use of delivery and misconduct-related mechanisms, while foundational governance mechanisms remain stable.Experience is positively associated with all accountability dimensions, indicating that accountability mechanisms become more prevalent as organizations accumulate AI project experience.The study contributes an empirically grounded framework of accountability mechanisms in AI projects and demonstrates that effective accountability requires mechanisms not only for governance and control but also for addressing the downstream consequences of AI system behavior.

title: Evaluation of pre-trained models for pedagogical assessment of novel AI-assisted educational questions
author_body: Michael Lawrence Castanares, Princess Ventures, Allan Tan
abstract: The surge in AI-assisted generation of educational materials has outpaced our capacity to validate their pedagogical quality. Automated evaluation using Bloom Classifier models is a promising approach to assess educational materials at scale. These models show high accuracy within-distribution dataset (IID Dataset). However, applying the same models to new out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets such as AI-assisted generated questions could show performance degradation. To identify robust classifiers under dataset shift, we evaluated traditional Machine Learning (ML), transformer, and Large Language models on the Bloom level classification task. We also explored feature-engineering strategies incorporating NLP metrics, appending the learning objectives as part of the input, and text splicing to stabilize OOD performance. Our baseline tests show that TFPOS-IDF ML models perform poorly on OOD (Macro F1-score 0.48) compared to BERT (0.55) and LLMs (0.79). Text splicing improved macro F1-score performance of ML and BERT models (0.59 and 0.62, respectively). Appending the learning objectives with the input increased model performance on specific dataset. Model retraining provided the largest improvement across models and datasets. Overall, these findings highlight the trade-off on the use of pre-trained models with novel AI-assisted educational questions and how strategic feature enhancements help address loss in performance.

title: Innovations in Design and Islamic-Value-Based Learning Models in the Digital Age: A Qualitative Study at MTS MAI Purwakarta
author_body: Acep Saepudin, Didin Nurul Rosidin, Taqiyuddin Taqiyuddin
abstract: s study examined the development of design innovations and Islamic-value-based learning models in addressing the challenges of the digital era at MTs MAI Purwakarta. The madrasah has distinctive characteristics due to its location within an Arab community that has developed since the colonial period, contributing to the formation of a strong Islamic educational tradition, particularly in Arabic language instruction, adab (Islamic manners), and the internalization of religious values. This study employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through field observations, in-depth interviews, and document reviews. The data were analyzed interactively through the processes of data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicate that learning innovations at MTs MAI Purwakarta focus not only on the integration of digital technology but also on strengthening historically rooted Islamic values. The learning design integrates cognitive, affective, and spiritual dimensions through value internalization in learning planning, the utilization of Islamic-content-based digital media, and religious habituation within the learning environment. The implemented learning models are adaptive, including blended learning and digital-based collaborative learning, while remaining guided by Islamic values of adab and ethics. The findings reveal a synthesis between the Islamic educational traditions of the Arab community and the demands of contemporary digital learning. This study contributes to the development of an integrative Islamic-value-based learning model that is contextual and relevant to education in the digital era.

title: Editorial: Generative AI and large language models in medicine: applications, challenges, and opportunities
author_body: Fahim Sufi, Seedahmed S. Mahmoud
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered medicine through a heterogeneous set of uses rather than through a single technological pathway. Large language models now draft clinical text, interpret reports, answer patient questions, support knowledge retrieval, structure health data, assist education, and participate in increasingly complex decision support workflows. The 34 contributions assembled in this Research Topic capture that breadth across clinical medicine, public health, digital health, oncology, rehabilitation, mental health, nursing, health informatics, education, quality management, and biomedical policy. Their collective value lies less in any single performance estimate than in the opportunity to examine what changes when language model research moves from demonstrations of linguistic competence toward systems that must operate under clinical constraints.The studies concerned with diagnosis, staging, and clinical reasoning show why this distinction matters. In a two institution study of 552 PET CT reports across six cancers, Xu et al. found that GPT 5 achieved 82.1 percent overall TNM staging accuracy compared with 77.0 percent for junior radiologists, while repeated model agreement was close to perfect. Performance nevertheless differed across cancer types and was weakest for metastatic staging. Dinç et al. reported an analogous pattern in radiation oncology. GPT 5 reached 92.8 percent on a standardized examination benchmark, substantially exceeding earlier GPT generations, yet authentic clinical vignettes still produced substantive errors in cases requiring precise trial knowledge or detailed adaptation to clinical context. The high benchmark score therefore did not remove the need for specialist review.Other studies reinforce the task dependent character of performance. Pan et al. found that DeepSeek V3.1, ChatGPT 5, and Grok 4 answered more than 90 percent of guideline derived bone cancer questions correctly in both evaluation rounds, although model specific strengths remained. In maternal venous thromboembolism care, Li et al. found superior overall expert ratings for GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek across education, care planning, and prevention, but explicitly did not interpret those results as evidence of readiness for independent nursing deployment. Konzmann et al., synthesizing 31 tumor board studies and 3,845 cases, identified a broader complexity gap: concordance was strongest in standardized and common oncological settings and deteriorated in rare, multimodal, or clinically ambiguous cases.This evidence is compatible with the conceptual position advanced by Greengrass, who treats AI as a potential support for human clinical reasoning rather than as a replacement for it. Human reasoning is constrained by working memory, cognitive load, fatigue, anchoring, and other biases, whereas computational systems can search and compare information at scales that exceed unaided cognition. The collection, however, does not support the inference that computational scale removes clinical uncertainty. Its more defensible implication is a risk gradient. Language models appear most reliable when the task has explicit rules, sufficiently complete textual evidence, and an auditable reference standard. Their reliability becomes more difficult to establish as the task requires multimodal interpretation, rare disease knowledge, rapidly changing evidence, patient specific tradeoffs, or judgments for which several clinically defensible answers may exist.A second theme concerns the architecture surrounding the language model. Several contributions suggest that the clinically relevant object is increasingly the full system rather than the foundation model in isolation. Barlow et al. fine-tuned an open Llama model to identify actionable incidental findings in PET CT reports and achieved a document level F1 score of 0.917 internally and 0.79 on an external test set. The reduction under external evaluation is itself informative, because differences in reporting style and institutional practice remain consequential even when internal performance is strong.Grounding methods address a different source of error. Kokash et al. combined ontology-based retrieval with LLM semantic adjudication for healthcare data harmonization and reported expert agreement as high as 92 percent. Retrieval alone was insufficient; the gain came from pairing broad candidate retrieval with model based semantic validation. Chen et al. provide a related demonstration through a knowledge graph system for Jin San Zhen therapy. Their hybrid architecture outperformed the general model on correctness, professionalism, and completeness, while the knowledge enhanced outputs remained traceable to source literature and no fabricated claims were detected in the evaluated question set. Sugihara et al. extend this architectural reasoning to the choice between open and proprietary models. Proprietary systems may offer stronger schema adherence or complex reasoning in some tasks, whereas open models provide advantages in local control, auditability, customization, privacy, and cost. The practical choice therefore depends on the clinical task and governance environment rather than on a universal model ranking.Bounded documentation and evidence processing tasks may be among the more defensible near term applications, but they still require verification. Aiumtrakul et al. found strong clinical reasoning in 89.7 percent of ChatGPT 5 generated nephrology prior authorization letters, yet diagnostic coding was correct in 79.3 percent and citation errors remained. Oami et al. observed high performance for background data extraction in systematic reviews, but outcome extraction was markedly more variable and repeated session consistency declined for the harder task. More elaborate prompting produced only modest accuracy changes while increasing processing time. Khoruzhaya et al. place these findings in methodological context: their review of medical text summarization reported external validation in only 7 percent of studies and patient safety assessment in only 3 percent, with wide variation in reported hallucination rates. Their MEDAI LLM SUMM checklist accordingly emphasizes clinical validity, prompt documentation, expert evaluation, hallucination assessment, safety, and data availability. Zhu et al., using eight models to generate medical examination questions and answers from real world EHRs, further show that models can approach clinicians on selected dimensions while human authors retain advantages in information sufficiency and overall answer quality.Taken together, these studies distinguish prompt engineering from clinical system engineering. Prompt design can improve instructions, but evidence grounding, model adaptation, structured outputs, local deployment, source traceability, safety rules, and expert adjudication determine whether an apparently competent model can be integrated into a reproducible workflow.Patient facing applications expose another limitation of accuracy centered evaluation. Graca et al. found that healthcare professionals rated ChatGPT responses more favourably than established evidence based PCOS responses for 11 of 12 questions, and further simplification improved readability. Yet the wider collection shows that medical correctness does not guarantee communicative usefulness. Joseph et al. found that cardiovascular responses changed in complexity with the education level implied by the prompt, but output frequently remained above ordinary health literacy needs. Wang et al. on gestational diabetes reported 92.17 percent mean accuracy for ChatGPT 5 on standardized questions and favourable reliability ratings, while all evaluated models still exceeded the recommended sixth grade reading level and showed poor transparency under JAMA criteria. Huang et al. reached a similar result for perinatal depression: responses were often informative and empathetic, but readability remained excessive and clinical safety behaviours were incomplete.The chronic heart failure study by Wang et al. on chronic heart failure adds actionability to this evaluation framework. Overall content quality was favourable, but median actionability was only 20 percent, and the most complete output was also among the least readable. This reveals a structural tradeoff that cannot be captured by accuracy alone. Albaz et al. likewise found favourable clarity and tone in ChatGPT 5 responses about vasectomy, but medical accuracy and completeness varied across questions and expert agreement was very low. Patient validation was absent. Angyal et al. approach the same problem from the user side by developing a questionnaire to measure how adults use ChatGPT for primary and secondary disease prevention, providing a basis for studying behaviour rather than assuming that availability translates into appropriate use.Two contributions show how patient and caregiver support may be made more constrained. Hanzawa et al. combined a domain specific knowledge base, retrieval augmented generation, sentiment analysis, explicit safety restrictions, and escalation rules in an agent supporting families implementing treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa. Experts rated 91.6 percent of 477 responses as clinically appropriate, but the authors appropriately call for usability testing and randomized evaluation of caregiver burden, adherence, and clinical outcomes. O'Malley et al. similarly describe retrieval, system instructions, and fine tuning as complementary strategies for customized physical activity chatbots, while emphasizing human evaluation, privacy, and operational cost.These studies support a multidimensional definition of patient facing quality. Accuracy and completeness remain necessary, but safe communication also requires readability, actionability, source traceability, uncertainty communication, cultural and educational fit, and evidence that users understand what the system has told them.Clinical implementation depends on professionals as well as models. Among Italian physiotherapists, Deodato et al. found widespread awareness of AI chatbots but limited clinical use: 66.9 percent had never used them in practice even though 78 percent expressed a positive attitude toward future adoption. Concerns centred on patient self diagnosis, false information, and loss of human interaction. In a sample drawn principally from Ecuador, Cherrez Ojeda et al. similarly found cautious optimism, but only 31.99 percent had used ChatGPT and 67.85 percent of familiar respondents regarded sole source clinical use as unethical. Safi et al. documented a different mismatch in surgical education: 80.9 percent had prior ChatGPT experience, yet 93.2 percent lacked formal AI training. Informal exposure is therefore advancing faster than structured professional education.The multimodal papers widen the definition of clinical AI while also illustrating why adding data modalities should not be assumed to improve performance. Manir et al. combined textual embeddings with acoustic summaries for affective tone analysis in aphasia. Under recording separated evaluation, the fused model did not outperform the text only model, and human agreement on aphasic affect was low. Hussain et al. review evidence in depression detection showing benefits from combining EEG, speech, facial, and linguistic signals, but also report the familiar decline from controlled laboratory results to more ecologically representative datasets. Siefert et al. demonstrate that smaller fine tuned models can approximate expert psychological ratings of complex narratives, particularly when model outputs are ensembled, yet they retain human supervision as the appropriate clinical frame.Multimodality also creates new risks. Jędrasiak and Bijoch examine synthetic audiovisual material in telemedicine and teledentistry, showing that manipulation can threaten diagnostic evidence, communication, and medico legal documentation. Their work makes provenance part of clinical safety. Trustworthy generative AI cannot be defined only by whether generated text is factually correct; healthcare systems must also be able to establish whether the data supplied to an AI system, or returned through a digital encounter, are authentic.The collection therefore shifts attention from model capability toward an evaluation and governance problem. Knott et al. show that healthcare AI studies still concentrate disproportionately on accuracy while paying far less attention to fairness, calibration, deployment readiness, and actual patient care. Their European analysis also makes clear that regulatory obligations depend on intended function and clinical risk. Administrative quality tools and systems that influence diagnosis or treatment cannot be governed as equivalent applications. Wang, Hao and Chen extend the accountability question into pharmaceutical intellectual property, where AI assisted discovery raises unresolved issues concerning inventorship, copyright, and ownership across jurisdictions.Reproducibility deserves particular attention. A clinical system that changes a medically material recommendation when the patient information has not changed poses a different problem from a deterministic medical device, even if its average performance is favourable. The tumor board literature synthesized by Konzmann et al. reports substantial variation in repeated response consistency and incomplete reporting of model inference settings across studies. Oami et al. likewise show that repeated session consistency can deteriorate as extraction becomes more complex. Model updates introduce another layer of temporal instability because the product evaluated today may not be behaviourally identical to the product deployed later.The evidence across the Research Topic supports a risk proportionate interpretation of human oversight. Lower consequence, reversible, and auditable tasks such as drafting, extraction, summarization, and guideline retrieval are plausible candidates for supervised implementation. Patient communication and guideline based decision support require stronger controls because deficiencies in readability, actionability, or omitted context may affect behaviour. Diagnosis, staging, treatment recommendation, and other high consequence applications require prospective validation, explicit uncertainty handling, and clinician accountability. Human review should therefore be designed into the workflow rather than appended as a generic disclaimer.Figure 1 represents this translational logic. Foundation model capability is only the first stage. Task adaptation must be followed by evidence grounding, workflow integration, clinical validation, and continuous governance. Human oversight, external validation, reproducibility, evidence traceability, health literacy and equity, privacy, and accountability operate across the pathway rather than at a single endpoint. This structure also explains why no universally superior medical language model emerges from the collection. Different systems lead on different endpoints, and the preferred model changes with the task, population, infrastructure, privacy requirements, and tolerance for error. The 34 contributions document a field moving from proof of language competence toward the science of accountable clinical integration. Contemporary models can perform useful work in structured clinical reasoning, data extraction, patient education, documentation, knowledge retrieval, psychological assessment, and administrative processes. They can sometimes match or exceed junior clinicians or established information sources on narrowly defined measures. Those findings are scientifically relevant, but they are not equivalent to evidence of autonomous clinical readiness.The next phase of research should therefore privilege prospective and multicentre evaluation, external validation across institutions and populations, repeated testing for response stability, explicit reporting of model versions and inference conditions, patient centred endpoints, economic evaluation, fairness assessment, and post deployment surveillance. Grounded architectures using curated retrieval, ontologies, knowledge graphs, local models, and explicit escalation rules warrant continued evaluation because they make model behaviour more constrained and auditable. Clinical AI literacy must develop in parallel so that professionals can judge uncertainty, verify sources, protect patient data, recognize inappropriate automation, and retain responsibility for consequential decisions.Generative AI is becoming useful in medicine before it has become uniformly trustworthy. The evidence in this Research Topic suggests that the appropriate response is neither unrestricted adoption nor categorical rejection. The defensible path is selective integration in which technical capability is matched to clinical risk, evidence is made traceable, validation extends beyond benchmark accuracy, and accountability remains explicit throughout the system lifecycle.

title: Bridging Legal, Financial, and Data Governance in Enterprise AI: Emerging Trends
author_body: Ashore-Onisemo Funmilayo
source_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
abstract: Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has moved faster than the institutional machinery meant to govern it. Within a single organization, an AI system is simultaneously a legal object subject to regulation and liability, a financial object subject to model risk management and audit, and a data object subject to lineage, quality, and privacy controls. These three governance domains (legal, financial, and data) have historically evolved in separate professional communities, with distinct vocabularies, control catalogues, and assurance rhythms. The result is fragmentation: overlapping obligations are duplicated, gaps between domains go unowned, and accountability becomes diffuse. This paper surveys the state of the art across the three domains and argues that their convergence is the defining governance trend for enterprise AI. We review advances in AI regulation and standards (the EU AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework), model risk management practice inherited from finance (notably SR 11-7), data governance frameworks (Abraham and colleagues; DAMA-DMBOK), and the maturing toolkit of documentation and explainability artefacts, including model cards, datasheets for datasets, and explainable AI methods. We propose a conceptual crosswalk that maps controls across domains onto shared AI lifecycle stages, exposing redundancy and gaps. We then examine open challenges (regulatory fragmentation, the pace of rule-making, unresolved liability allocation, and cross-border friction) and set out a research agenda for integrated governance that treats legal, financial, and data controls as a single accountable system rather than three parallel ones. The contribution is a synthesis and an organizing frame intended to guide both practitioners and future scholarship.

title: Integrating generative artificial intelligence in education: perspectives of in-service and pre-service educators in the Belgrade metropolitan area
author_body: Danimir Mandić, Gordana Miščević, Ivica Radovanović, Filip Kojić
abstract: This study examined the perceptions of in-service and pre-service educators regarding the opportunities and challenges associated with the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in education. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with a diverse sample of 797 participants (20.8% men, 79.2% women) from the Belgrade metropolitan area, Serbia, including preschool and school teachers, university professors, and pre-service educators (students enrolled in faculties of education). An author-developed questionnaire was used to assess reported use of GAI tools, perceived contributions to teaching and learning, ethical considerations, and professional readiness. While 39% of participants reported using GAI tools, the majority reported no use of specific GAI tools in their educational practice. The highest-rated aspect of GAI concerned the need for clearly defined ethical guidelines, whereas perceived relevance for supporting students socio-emotional development and critical thinking was comparatively low. Overall perceptions of GAI across the domains covered by the questionnaire were moderate (M = 2.97), reflecting cautious openness among in-service and pre-service educators. Perceptions varied significantly across socio-demographic characteristics, with more favorable evaluations reported by participants with fewer than 10 years of professional experience and by university-based educators and students. The findings highlight the central role of ethical governance and professional readiness in shaping in-service and pre-service educators’ evaluations of GAI and point to the importance of targeted professional development and institutional support for context-appropriate integration of GAI in educational practice.

title: Nuclear and Renewable Energy Transitions for Global Sustainability: Exploring the Interactions of Tourism Development and Economic Drivers
author_body: Tuba Rasheed, Mahwish Zafar, Hamza Akram, Muhammad Farhan Bashir, Muhammad Sadiq, Miao Ye
abstract: ABSTRACT In light of exacerbating climate change issues, recent environmental policy reforms have attempted to balance economic growth and environmental conservation to foster a sustainable development transition. To further debate the scope of decarbonization policies, this study investigates the long‐run effects of tourism, nuclear energy, financial markets, economic growth, renewable energy transition, and urbanization on ecological footprint and load capacity factor in nuclear‐energy‐dependent countries. This research relies on extended econometric analysis to reveal that tourism, nuclear power, financial markets, renewable energy transition, and urbanization considerably lower economic growth but exacerbate ecological footprints. We also reveal that tourism, nuclear energy, financial markets, and renewable energy transition have a detrimental impact on the load capacity factor, whereas the opposite is true for economic growth and urbanization. The empirical findings allow us to determine that an integrated policy framework involving renewable energy, a sustainable economic and tourism agenda, and smart urban planning is essential for long‐term environmental sustainability.

title: Governance-as-Code: Translating EU AI Act Technical Requirements into Executable Compliance Pipelines for Generative AI Systems
author_body: Rudrendu Kumar Paul, Sourav Nandy
abstract: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) imposes technical obligations on high-risk AI providers, yet Articles 8-15 were drafted for predictive AI and leave seven technical gaps when applied to generative systems, spanning non-deterministic data governance, training-data provenance, continuous conformity, human oversight, open-ended robustness, emergent risk, and generative fairness. We deliver Governance-as-Code (GaC), a framework of 43 machine-checkable acceptance criteria across six compliance modules that run in a CI/CD pipeline and emit Article-indexed audit evidence, and we show the actual Rego policy code rather than merely describing it. Our central commitment is that the Act's open-textured standards ("appropriate levels," "possible biases") become declared, auditable numbers: robustness thresholds are derived from the provider's documented baseline and a state-of-the-art floor, and framing bias is collapsed into eight measurable proxies tested by counterfactual demographic probing. We also correct who owes what, since under Article 25 and Chapter V a downstream deployer relies on the upstream provider's Article 53 training-data summary and documents only the layers it controls, so GaC verifies that summary rather than demanding per-sample documentation the deployer never had. We validate on two enterprise deployments, a high-risk advisory chatbot and a limited-risk content generator, benchmarking against a manual expert audit rather than documentation artifacts that were never designed to enforce compliance. GaC reproduces all of the manual audit's findings, including three penalty-triggering violations, while cutting audit labor by roughly 75%.

title: The Interplay between Socio-Ethical, Legal and Technological Standards in Developing Automated Law Enforcement Systems: The Case of AI-Enabled Crime Analytics
author_body: Anastasia Kordoni, Athina Sachoulidou, Cristina Rego de Oliveira
abstract: Enabling technologies, including but not limited to artificial intelligence (AI), may have the potential to revolutionise how LEAs operate, but often this comes along with concerns for fundamental rights. The need for a careful balancing act has already been reflected in the contents of the EU AI Act – with the use of AI for law enforcement purposes becoming –not surprisingly– the ‘apple of discord’ during the trilogue negotiations. These debates made it prevalent that normative standards alone may be insufficient if not combined with creative technical design solutions that will be inspired by human rights considerations and translate abstract ethical values and normative standards into tangible results. Driven by this, this chapter first discusses the implications of automated law enforcement –with a focus on AI-enabled crime analytics– for fundamental procedural rights. Second, it scrutinises the EU approach to AI-enabled crime analytics as crystallised in the final text of the EU AI Act. Third, it argues in favour of integrating socio-ethical and normative standards with technical design solutions, elucidating this intricate process through a ‘matching exercise.’ Finally, it informs a socio-ethical approach to AI-enabled crime analytics on the basis of bias detection and mitigation to address the (organisational) realities of automated law enforcement. By addressing the interplay between socio-ethical, legal and technological standards, this chapter contributes to a holistic understanding of the implications and governance of AI-powered crime analytics, fostering a multi-disciplinary discourse at the crossroads of automation and law enforcement.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
author_body: Tao Huang, Guosen Wu, Guolong Zheng, Jiayang Meng, Chen Hou, Xu Yang, Xuechao Yang, Feng Xia
abstract: Privacy leakage in LLM agents is commonly evaluated within individual components such as memory, retrieval, or tool-use pipelines, which makes it difficult to distinguish internal exposure from information that an external observer can actually recover. We present CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channel-aware evaluation framework for black-box privacy leakage in LLM agents. CIPL represents a target through sensitive source, selection, assembly, execution, observation, and extraction stages and evaluates the transition from selected sensitive units to attacker-recoverable output under a shared protocol. Experiments across memory-based, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated targets, together with a BrowserUse live-agent case study, show that storage labels alone do not determine recoverability. Memory targets form a near-saturated reference case, retrieval-mediated leakage is frequently partial, and tool-mediated and live-agent leakage varies strongly with observation surface, prompt-to-channel alignment, retrieval depth, and provider behavior. A stratified semantic audit further identifies attacker-useful disclosures that canonical exact matching misses. CIPL therefore provides a common framework for comparing how internal sensitive dependence is realized as externally recoverable leakage across heterogeneous agent pipelines.

title: Designing Trustworthy Agentic AI Systems for Autonomous Decision-Making: A Framework for Safety, Explainability, Security, and Accountability
author_body: Dr.   Pankaj Kumar
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has led to a new generation of systems known as agentic AI, which can perceive information, reason about objectives, plan tasks, use digital tools, and perform actions with limited human intervention. Unlike conventional AI applications that primarily generate predictions or content, agentic AI systems can operate through multi-step decision-making processes and interact with external environments. This increased autonomy creates significant opportunities in healthcare, education, cybersecurity, finance, public administration, and software engineering, but it also introduces new risks related to safety, security, transparency, privacy, and accountability. This paper proposes a framework for designing trustworthy agentic AI systems based on four central principles: safety, explainability, security, and accountability. The study examines the major challenges associated with autonomous decision-making and presents a conceptual framework integrating human oversight, risk assessment, explainable reasoning, continuous monitoring, secure tool use, auditability, and governance. Analytical tables are used to compare risks, mitigation strategies, trust dimensions, and evaluation criteria. The paper argues that trustworthy agentic AI should not be designed merely as a more capable form of automation; rather, it should be developed as a controlled socio-technical system in which autonomy is proportional to risk and human oversight remains meaningful. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for future research and practical implementation of responsible autonomous AI systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence as an Economic, Environmental, Geopolitical, and Social Transformation
author_body: Marcin Marciniak
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence is often discussed primarily as a technological breakthrough. Such an approach is insufficient because AI is also transforming the allocation of capital, energy, natural resources, labour, and political power. Investment in generative AI and computing infrastructure is increasing rapidly and is increasingly concentrated among a small number of corporations and countries. At the same time, the expansion of data centres creates new electricity and water demands, potentially producing local infrastructure bottlenecks and distributive conflicts. The AI value chain is dependent on geographically concentrated supplies of advanced semiconductors, manufacturing equipment, cloud services, energy, and specialised knowledge. Control over these bottlenecks may give states and corporations structural power that does not derive directly from military superiority. The environmental effects of AI are similarly ambivalent: AI systems consume energy, water, materials, and computing hardware, but may also improve energy efficiency, climate modelling, renewable-energy integration, and environmental monitoring. Finally, AI-enabled automation, including intelligent robotics, may reduce employment in some occupations while augmenting labour and creating new tasks in others. The social outcome of this transformation will therefore depend not only on the technology itself but also on competition policy, infrastructure planning, environmental regulation, social protection, collective bargaining, and the distribution of productivity gains.

title: **The Paradox of Artificial Intelligence: Capabilities, Limitations, and the Illusion of Autonomy in Modern AI Systems — A Critical Analysis of Narrow AI, Data Dependency, and the Imperative for Human Oversight**
author_body: Sudhakar Geruganti
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: --- ## Alternative Titles 1. **"Nenu Swatantrudini!" (I Am Independent!): Deconstructing the Myth of AI Autonomy and the Reality of Human Dependency**2. **The Myth of the Thinking Machine: Why Artificial Intelligence Is Not Independent, Conscious, or Objective**3. **Beyond the Hype: A Critical Examination of AI's Capabilities, Ethical Dilemmas, and the Illusion of Autonomy**4. **Artificial Intelligence and the Illusion of Independence: Data Bias, Algorithmic Opacity, and the Human-in-the-Loop Imperative**5. **From Narrow AI to Ethical AI: Understanding the True Nature, Limitations, and Societal Impact of Intelligent Systems**6. **The Emperor's New Algorithm: How AI's "Independence" Masks Human Design, Data Bias, and Accountability Gaps**7. **Rethinking Artificial Intelligence: Autonomy, Ethics, and the Case for Responsible Human-Centric AI Governance** --- ## Subtitles 1. **Why Current AI Systems Lack True Consciousness, Self-Awareness, and Independent Agency**2. **A Critical Analysis of Narrow AI, Large Language Models, and the Probabilistic Nature of Machine "Intelligence"**3. **Examining Data Dependency, Algorithmic Bias, and the Ethical Challenges of Deploying AI in Society**4. **The Case for Human-in-the-Loop Governance in an Age of Generative AI and Autonomous Systems**5. **Distinguishing Between Simulated Understanding and Genuine Comprehension in Artificial Intelligence**6. **From Job Displacement to Deepfakes: The Societal Risks of Over-Reliance on AI Without Human Oversight**7. **AI as a Tool, Not a Master: Ensuring Responsible Development and Deployment of Intelligent Technologies** --- ## Detailed Description ### Overview This research paper critically examines the fundamental nature of Artificial Intelligence (AI), challenging the widespread misconception that AI systems possess true autonomy, consciousness, or independent thought. Drawing inspiration from the provocative Telugu article **"Nenu Swatantrudini!"** ("I Am Independent!"), the paper deconstructs the narrative that AI can think, reason, and act independently of human direction. It argues that current AI systems—including advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, as well as Generative AI tools—are sophisticated **probabilistic engines** that simulate understanding through statistical pattern recognition, but lack genuine comprehension, intentionality, or self-awareness. The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of AI's capabilities and limitations, emphasizing the critical distinction between **Narrow AI** (task-specific systems) and the hypothetical **Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)** . It explores the ethical, social, and practical implications of AI deployment, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, job displacement, misinformation, and autonomous weapons. Ultimately, it advocates for a **Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)** approach to AI governance, ensuring that critical decisions retain human judgment, transparency, and accountability. ### The Core Problem: The Illusion of Autonomy The central thesis of this paper is that AI's perceived "independence" is an illusion. Every AI system operates within boundaries defined by:- **Training Data:** AI models are only as good as the data they are trained on. If that data contains historical biases (racial, gender, socio-economic), the AI will perpetuate and amplify those biases.- **Algorithmic Design:** AI systems function as "black boxes." Even their creators cannot fully explain how deep learning networks arrive at specific decisions.- **Human Intent:** AI does not possess goals, desires, or intentions. It executes tasks based on human-defined objectives and reward functions. The paper argues that conflating AI's computational power with human-like intelligence is not only philosophically flawed but also dangerous, as it leads to over-reliance on AI for decisions that require ethical reasoning, empathy, and contextual understanding. ### Key Themes and Analysis **1. Narrow AI vs. General Intelligence**- Current AI is **Narrow AI**, designed for specific tasks (e.g., recommendation algorithms, chatbots, predictive analytics).- It lacks **general intelligence**—the ability to reason, learn, and apply knowledge across diverse domains, as humans do.- The paper distinguishes between **simulated understanding** (AI generating coherent text) and **genuine comprehension** (human understanding of meaning and context). **2. The Data Dependency Problem**- AI systems are fundamentally dependent on vast datasets, raising concerns about: - **Bias and Discrimination:** Perpetuation of historical inequalities. - **Data Privacy:** Commodification of personal information without consent. - **Algorithmic Opacity:** The "black box" problem in deep learning. **3. Ethical and Societal Implications**- **Job Displacement:** Automation threatens workers in manufacturing, customer service, and transportation.- **Misinformation and Deepfakes:** Generative AI can produce highly realistic fake content, undermining democratic processes and public trust.- **Autonomous Weapons:** Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) raise profound ethical and legal questions about accountability.- **Economic Inequality:** The benefits of AI may accrue disproportionately to developed nations and corporations, exacerbating global disparities. **4. The Human-in-the-Loop Imperative**The paper advocates for a **Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)** approach, which includes:- **Human Oversight:** Critical decisions in healthcare, law, and defense must retain human judgment.- **Transparency:** AI systems should be explainable and auditable.- **Accountability:** Clear lines of responsibility for AI-driven outcomes.- **Education:** Public awareness of AI's capabilities and limitations to counter misinformation and undue awe. ### The Indian and Global Context While the paper is global in scope, it contextualizes its arguments within the Indian landscape, where AI adoption is rapidly expanding through initiatives like **Digital India, Aadhaar, UPI, and the IndiaAI Mission**. It highlights the unique challenges faced by developing economies, including:- **Infrastructure Gaps:** Limited access to computing resources and high-speed internet.- **Skill Shortages:** Need for AI literacy and ethical training.- **Regulatory Frameworks:** Absence of comprehensive AI governance policies.- **Digital Divide:** Risk of marginalized communities being left behind. The paper argues that India, like other nations, must develop AI responsibly—ensuring that its benefits are shared equitably and its risks are mitigated through robust policy and ethical guidelines. ### Proposed Solutions and Recommendations From a **materials science and engineering perspective**, the paper proposes several strategies for responsible AI development: 1. **Ethical AI Design:** Embedding ethical considerations into the AI development lifecycle.2. **Bias Auditing:** Regular assessment of AI models for discriminatory outcomes.3. **Data Governance:** Transparent data collection, consent mechanisms, and privacy protections.4. **Explainable AI (XAI):** Developing AI systems that can explain their decisions in human-understandable terms.5. **Human-Centric AI:** Prioritizing human well-being, dignity, and autonomy in AI deployment.6. **International Cooperation:** Global frameworks for AI governance, including bans on lethal autonomous weapons.7. **Education and Awareness:** Integrating AI ethics and critical thinking into educational curricula. ### Conclusion: AI as a Tool, Not a Master The paper concludes with a powerful assertion: **AI is not independent. It is a tool created by humans, for humans.** Its "intelligence" is a reflection of human intelligence, and its "autonomy" is constrained by human design. The real question is not whether AI will become independent, but whether humans will use AI responsibly. The title **"Nenu Swatantrudini!"** ("I Am Independent!") serves as a provocative metaphor—a warning against the hubris of attributing human-like qualities to machines. The future of AI depends on our ability to govern it wisely, ensuring that it serves human flourishing rather than undermining it. The independence of AI is a myth; the responsibility for its impact lies squarely with humanity. ### Target Audience This paper is intended for:- **Researchers and academics** in computer science, artificial intelligence, ethics, and philosophy.- **Policymakers and government officials** involved in AI governance, technology regulation, and digital policy.- **Technology industry professionals** working on AI development, deployment, and ethics.- **Educators and students** in engineering, computer science, and social sciences.- **Civil society organizations** advocating for digital rights, privacy, and ethical technology.- **General readers** interested in understanding the true nature and impact of AI. ### Keywords Artificial Intelligence; Narrow AI; Machine Learning; Large Language Models; Autonomy; Consciousness; Ethics; Data Privacy; Algorithmic Bias; Human-in-the-Loop; AI Governance; Deepfakes; Autonomous Weapons; Digital India; Responsible AI --- ## Suggested Citation Sudhakar, G. title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Literacy Education
author_body: Emerald Publishing Limited
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is rapidly reshaping education, assisting teachers in planning, resource creation, and assessment while students increasingly engage with AI for learning and text construction. Despite restrictions on GenAI use in schools, its presence is undeniable, prompting urgent questions about its role in literacy education. Since the introduction of ChatGPT in 2023, research has surged on AI’s impact on higher education and foreign language instruction. However, the intersection of GenAI and literacy education for school-aged students (K-12) remains underexplored. This essential volume examines AI-assisted learning, student engagement with AI-generated texts, and the implications for literacy educators as GenAI becomes more powerful and accessible. Furthermore, it explores the evolving responsibilities of teachers as AI supports professional learning, planning, and assessment. With GenAI’s dynamic and expanding capabilities, Generative Artificial Intelligence in Literacy Education offers timely insights into the future of literacy education. A must-read for educators, researchers, and policymakers seeking to navigate the complex relationship between artificial intelligence and the teaching of reading and writing in K-12 schools.

title: Governance Is a Runtime Dependency: An Evidence Map and Operational AI Readiness Matrix for Disaster Management
author_body: Sandip Patel, Deependra Singh Rawat, Bhavin Gandecha
abstract: Disaster-management AI is commonly governed before deployment through ethics reviews, data-sharing agreements, and standards checklists.This paper argues that design-time governance is necessary but incomplete because decisive failures occur while systems run: a prediction must be overridden, a model rolled back, a decision audited, an incident escalated, or a system kept safe when connectivity degrades.We reframe governance as a runtime dependency and synthesize a purposively screened 80-record set of standards, policy documents, surveys, primary studies, and technical sources.Ten runtime controls are coded through 232 nonexclusive source-control assignments.Coverage averages 23.2 sources per control (median 21.5; range 6 to 43); the five mostcovered controls account for 80.2% of assignments, whereas the five least-covered controls account for 19.8%.A six-family standards crosswalk contains support in 31 of 60 cells (51.7%), with each control represented by two to four instrument families and no family covering all controls.Auditability, coproduction, and human override are prominent, while ownership, rollback, incident reporting, and degraded-mode operation remain comparatively sparse.The contribution is an Operational AI Readiness Matrix with pass/fail questions, evidence requirements, and four maturity levels.An analytical evaluation checks completeness, traceability, maturity discrimination, non-compensation, and scenario coverage, while explicitly recognizing that the matrix has not yet been validated against deployment outcomes.The result is a practical instrument for testing whether disaster-AI systems remain governable during drills and live events, not merely documented before use.

title: PriMobiBench: Characterizing Visual Privacy Leakage in VLM-Driven Mobile GUI Agents
author_body: Qihang Cen, Tianshuo Cong, Da Song, Xinlei He, Jiaxing Song, Ke Xu, Qi Li
abstract: Mobile GUI agents increasingly rely on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to automate smartphone tasks by interpreting screenshot streams. However, this design introduces serious and underexplored privacy risks, including direct leakage of sensitive on-screen information and unintended user profiling. The absence of standardized benchmarks makes it difficult to quantify these risks in realistic mobile agent workflows. To address this gap, we propose PriMobiBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating privacy leakage and visual profiling in screenshot-driven mobile agents. It provides a unified pipeline for data generation, agent trajectory construction, and multi-model evaluation. We also introduce MobiLeak, a dataset of execution traces from 16 apps, covering 25 privacy attributes with 2,960 embedded privacy instances. Our results reveal substantial risks: (1) VLMs can directly extract sensitive information with up to 82.5% success rate; (2) beyond explicit leakage, they can infer user profiles from aggregated visual evidence with approximately 70% success. We further propose a mitigation that masks privacy-sensitive but task-irrelevant UI elements before cloud processing, reducing profiling success by up to 58% with only approximately 8% performance loss. Overall, our work provides the first systematic benchmark for visual privacy risks in mobile GUI agents, demonstrates that both leakage and profiling are feasible at a highly concerning level, and offers a practical direction for mitigation.

title: Student Co-Created Formative Assessment in a Cross-Disciplinary Data Literacy Module: A Microcurricula Approach at Scale
author_body: Yalemisew Abgaz
source_name: Dublin City University Open Access Institutional Repository (Dublin City University)
abstract: Designing inclusive and engaging formative assessments at scale across heterogeneous programmes remains a persistent challenge in higher education (Andersson & Palm, 2017; King, 2022). This challenge is amplified as data literacy and analytics emerge as critical transversal competencies across all disciplines in an AI-shaped graduate landscape (Reynolds et al., 2020). Yet instructor-designed assessments dominate at scale, lacking student perspective and inclusivity. To our knowledge, no prior study has examined student co-creation of formative assessment within a cross-disciplinary microcurricula framework at institutional scale. This paper presents a co-creation intervention within a microcurricula module (a modular cross-faculty design serving 15+ programmes across five faculties) in which high-performing students from the previous cohort co-designed formative assessments, enabling prospective students to learn directly from peer strategies and experience. These were offered as optional preparation resources for summative assessment across seven Data Literacy and Analytics Topics (Abgaz, 2026; Abgaz & Dunne, 2023) with this research focusing on two practice-heavy, technology-oriented topics. Among 1,432 and 1,387 enrolled students per topic, 392 and 216 respectively engaged with the co-created assessments. Independent samples t-tests revealed a statistically significant improvement (p < .05) across both topics. Thematic analysis of student feedback further revealed enhanced metacognitive awareness and increased confidence in assessment preparedness, reinforcing the value of peer-designed resources in cross-disciplinary learning. These findings position student co-created formative assessment as a scalable, equity-aligned strategy for cross-disciplinary STEM education. In doing so, they reposition students as active agents and co-owners of the learning process, with implications for equitable curriculum design across higher education.

title: Transforming Literacy Education With AI in Developing Countries: Challenges and Future Prospects
author_body: Munazza Jabeen
source_name: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Literacy Education
abstract: Abstract This chapter addresses the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in formal education settings in resource-limited developing countries. Access to high-quality literacy learning and basic literacy skills remains unequal in developing countries. This study used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework to systematically review articles published between 2020 and 2025, resulting in a final sample of 26. Thematic analysis identified three key themes. First, AI is transforming literacy education by enhancing reading and writing skills, enabling personalised learning, supporting teachers and promoting equity and inclusion. Second, major barriers to adoption in developing countries include unstable power supply, limited internet access, high costs, insufficient teacher training and unreliable government structures. Third, building equitable ecosystems requires strengthening teacher capabilities, developing culturally and linguistically inclusive resources, implementing low-bandwidth solutions, establishing supportive policies, fostering public–private partnerships and securing sustainable funding. These findings show that while AI has significant potential, technological advancement is concentrated in specific countries, leaving many disadvantaged regions marginalised. The research indicates that AI adopts a dual function. It can enhance learning, stimulate creativity and foster inclusion. This study underscores the convergence of infrastructure, pedagogy, equity and policy, adding to knowledge about the conditions necessary for AI to be successfully applied in literacy teaching and learning in schools/formal education operating in resource-limited environments in developing countries.
